data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["Git objects are content-addressed and immutable; event log entries are append-only but not independently addressable in the same way\u2014they form a sequence, not a DAG.","Git truncation means losing a commit; event log truncation means losing causal state, which may not be reconstructable from the remaining prefix if the lost event carried irreducible state.","Git's tree structure is designed for branching; an event log is linear, so the MMR adds complexity without the branching benefit."],"overturn_conditions":["If the reasoning system's event log is inherently linear (each event references exactly one predecessor) and cannot be restructured as a tree without losing the append-only semantics, the MMR approach is inapplicable.","If the cost of audit is not the binding constraint on refusal policy (i.e., the system refuses for correctness reasons regardless of audit cost), then cheaper verification does not change the refusal policy."],"shared_structure":["Both MMR-based logs and git's object store use tree-structured hashes that allow localized integrity verification without recomputing the entire history.","Both allow truncation of a corrupt tail by dropping the affected subtree rather than rewriting the entire chain."],"source_memory_refs":["SCR_003"],"transfer_claims":["The principle of localized verification transfers: if the event log uses a tree-structured identity, the cost of crash-halt audit drops from O(n) to O(log n), which may shift the practical policy from 'always refuse crash halts' to 'audit then decide,' even though the logical resumability conditions are unchanged."]},"claim":"Resumability conditions depend on the log's identity structure: with a linear hash chain, a partial write at the tail can only be detected by recomputing the entire chain (O(n)), which makes audit expensive and incentivizes blanket refusal for any uncertain halt. With a Merkle mountain range (MMR) or similar tree-structured identity, tail integrity can be verified in O(log n), and a corrupt tail event can be truncated safely by removing only the affected peak\u2014making crash-halt resumption practical rather than prohibitively expensive, and thus changing the refusal policy from 'always refuse crash halts' to 'refuse only if audit reveals untruncatable corruption.'","counterconditions":[{"case":"MMR truncation removes not just the corrupt event but all events in the same peak, potentially discarding valid committed events alongside the partial one\u2014this is data loss, not clean resumption.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the partial write corrupts a lower peak (not just the tail), the MMR structure cannot isolate it without recomputing from the base, collapsing back to O(n).","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the storage layer does not support atomic writes at MMR-peak granularity, the physical write boundaries may not align with MMR structure boundaries, making peak-level truncation infeasible.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"The cost of verification (O(log n) vs O(n)) does not change the logical resumability conditions\u2014only the practical cost of the audit step. A system that refuses crash halts for correctness reasons (not cost) would still refuse them with an MMR.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"In a linear hash chain H_i = hash(H_{i-1} || E_i), any tail corruption requires walking the full chain to confirm where integrity breaks. With an MMR, each event contributes to log-height peaks; the root can be recomputed from peaks in O(log n), and a corrupted peak can be dropped, truncating the log to the previous valid state at that peak. This means that even for crash halts, the system can cheaply identify and excise the partial write, then resume from the verified prefix\u2014provided the storage layer can identify which physical writes belong to which MMR peak.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
